Keywords: Morning Mist Ambush at Lake Trasimene
RagShortTexts: In 217 BC Hannibal used the morning mist on the shore of Lake Trasimene to lay a tight ambush, destroying thirty thousand Roman legionaries and killing the consul Flaminius.

Variants.Content: In the spring of 217 BC Hannibal led his army south through the Tuscan marshes into Etruria, deliberately burning estates along the way to lure the newly elected Roman consul Gaius Flaminius into a reckless advance. Hannibal concealed his troops in the wooded hills above a narrow defile on the northern shore of Lake Trasimene. At dawn a thick mist that blotted out the sky lay over the lake, and Flaminius's legions blundered into the long trap before they could form battle lines. The trumpets sounded the charge: Gallic warriors swept down on the flank, while Spanish infantry and Numidian cavalry sealed the entrance and the line of retreat. In less than three hours fifteen thousand Roman soldiers lay dead on the lakeshore or drowned among the reeds; the consul Flaminius was beheaded by a Gallic horseman, and the six thousand men of the vanguard were all taken prisoner. When the news reached Rome, a praetor announced to the terrified crowd in the Forum only one grim sentence: "We have been defeated in a great battle."

Lake Trasimene is a wound of blood and tears that Rome will never forget. The consul Flaminius, a man of the popular faction, was arrogant and conceited; he not only scorned the Senate but before setting out openly ignored the evil omen of the sacred chickens refusing their feed. Because of this blind rush for glory, two entire elite Roman legions were driven into a death trap by the Carthaginians' base trick of the morning mist, and thousands of young soldiers were herded into the lake and drowned before they could even draw their short swords. The battle shocked the Senate and forced Rome to declare a state of emergency throughout its territory and to name the veteran Fabius dictator, to keep the city from falling into irreversible ruin.

The Battle of Lake Trasimene is Hannibal's masterpiece of war, in which he mastered both the fine details of the terrain and the mind of the enemy commander. Hannibal saw at a glance the impatient, rash character of Flaminius the popular politician, and used the dense lake mist and the narrow pass between hills and water to set a perfect trap. When the order to strike was given, Carthage's warriors of many peoples fell upon the enemy like soldiers sent from heaven and cut the heavy, crowded Roman formation into several pieces. This battle not only won a glorious victory, destroying more than twenty thousand enemies at minimal cost, but also shattered Rome's defensive line in the northern Apennines and threw open the rich southern lands on the road to Rome.
